text:
Governments cannot build everything at once, and opinions differ on whether public spending on transport should be focused on public transport or on roads. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of public transport argue that it serves more people per unit of space. Trains and buses carry many passengers with less pollution and help those without cars. A single metro line, for example, can move as many commuters as several motorways, and it takes cars off the streets. Cities that invest in public transport suffer less congestion and air pollution, and they offer mobility to the poor, the young and the elderly. Since transport produces a large share of greenhouse gases, shifting passengers to trains and buses also supports climate targets. New roads, in contrast, often attract more traffic and soon become full again.

On the other hand, supporters of roads argue that they remain essential for goods and remote areas. Freight, rural communities and emergency services depend on good roads. A farmer who needs to deliver milk to the market, or an ambulance that has to reach a village, cannot rely on a train. In regions with few people, public transport is expensive and rarely used, whereas well-built roads give everyone access. Buses also need good roads to run on. Maintaining existing roads prevents accidents and costly damage to vehicles.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that spending should depend on local needs, but in most cities public transport should receive priority, while rural areas need continued investment in roads.

Thiết yếu cho hàng hoá và vùng xa: vận tải, nông thôn, cấp cứu; ví dụ nông dân giao sữa, xe cấp cứu đến làng; vùng ít dân GTCC đắt ít dùng; buýt cũng cần đường tốt; bảo trì ngăn tai nạn.
